clue.text: Pet butterfly?

definitions.meaning: to pet an animal is to run a hand gently along it
the butterfly is one of the swimming styles, alongside crawl and breaststroke

explanation.surface: Someone wondering whether a pet could be called a butterfly.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: a gentle caress of the hand, and a named swimming technique such as the butterfly.

clue.text: Method of colouring or drawing fatal, it's said?

indicators.note: it's said tells us the letters follow how the phrase sounds

parts.note: a draw is a tie, and a fatal end is to die, so the phrase is 'tie and die'

explanation.surface: A question about colouring, or else about a deadly draw.
explanation.definitionFit: A way of patterning cloth by knotting it before soaking it in colour is a method of colouring.

clue.text: Work as deejay, say and may do 3 visiting hours

parts.note: OP is short for opus, a work

parts.words: as deejay, say and may do 3
parts.note: the words deejay, say and may each end in the letters A and Y, so they end AY, which is what this part of the light spells

explanation.surface: A radio presenter's working routine, hinting at hours when visitors are welcome.
explanation.walkthrough: The '3' is a cross-reference to this very clue: deejay, say and may do what 3 spells after OP, i.e. they END AY.
explanation.definitionFit: A day when a school or institution admits the public is a time set aside for visiting.

clue.text: Put up feet on so idyllic village green

indicators.note: put up in a down clue means the letters are raised, read from bottom to top
in a down clue the foot of a word is its last letter, so the feet of these words are their final letters

explanation.surface: Relaxing with feet up on an idyllic village green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up feet' suggests resting, but it signals the last letters of so, idyllic and village (OCE), turned upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Green in the environmental sense is ecological, and the short prefix-like form is used for that.

clue.text: Like bankers from America, back to start afresh

indicators.note: back says the two letters for America are read the other way round

parts.note: to refire an engine or kiln is to start it up again

explanation.surface: A comment on American bankers returning to square one.
explanation.walkthrough: In betting a banker is a selection thought certain to win, so bankers are dead certs, not financiers.
explanation.definitionFit: A banker in racing slang is a near-certain winner, and something certain to succeed is described by this hyphenated adjective.

clue.text: Girl sat, with time to go for a dip

parts.note: Sal is a girl's name, short for Sally

indicators.note: to go means the time letter is removed from the word sat

explanation.surface: A girl sitting down before going for a swim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dip' suggests a swim, but it is a sauce to dip food into.
explanation.definitionFit: A spicy Mexican-style sauce often served with tortilla chips as a dip.

clue.text: Event for skater or curler and US bowler

parts.note: a roller is a hair curler
Americans call a bowler hat a derby

explanation.surface: A sporting event catering for skaters, curlers and American cricket bowlers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'curler' and 'bowler' look like sportspeople, but they are a hair roller and a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A contact sport raced on wheeled skates round a track is an event for skaters.

clue.text: Founder bringing in new man for supporters' club post, maybe

indicators.note: bringing in puts the rearranged letters inside the failing word

parts.note: to founder is to fail, as a ship sinks

indicators.note: new signals a fresh arrangement of the letters of man

explanation.surface: The founder of a supporters' club bringing in a new man to run its post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Founder' looks like the person who started the club, but it is the verb meaning collapse; 'new' gives NMA from MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Letters sent by admirers, such as a supporters' club, are post of this kind.

clue.text: Case of demi-sec certainly tipped up

indicators.note: tipped up says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A wine buff on a demi-sec champagne, certainly worth recommending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' looks like a box of wine, but it is the slang verb to case a place, i.e. scout it.
explanation.definitionFit: To case a joint is to look it over beforehand, which is to reconnoitre or scout.

clue.text: Little room by enclosure for one returning breeding stock

indicators.note: returning says the whole string of pieces is read backwards

parts.note: the little room is a coy name for the toilet, the loo
a pen is an enclosure for animals
for one means for example, abbreviated eg

explanation.surface: An estate agent's description of a small room next to a paddock, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns the whole run round, not just the last piece; 'Little room' is the toilet, a British euphemism.
explanation.definitionFit: The total stock of inherited variation in an interbreeding population is what a breeder draws on, hence breeding stock.

clue.text: Folly of fine material a Parisian installed

indicators.note: installed means placed inside, so the French word goes within the lace word

parts.note: lacy describes something made of delicate lace
a Parisian would say un for a

explanation.surface: A Parisian fitting delicate fabric, and it proving a foolish idea.
explanation.definitionFit: Folly is foolishness, and madness or extreme foolishness is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Wanting Queen at aid gathering afresh

indicators.note: gathering the letters afresh means collecting them into a new order

explanation.surface: A queen falling short as she collects help again.
explanation.definitionFit: Wanting in the sense of lacking or not good enough is a synonym of insufficient.

clue.text: Ancient craft that in France and Middle East's retained in doubt briefly

indicators.note: retained means held inside, so the in and doubt pieces sit within the French and Middle East letters

parts.note: que is French for that
taken as written

indicators.note: briefly cuts the last letter off the doubt word

parts.note: a query is a doubt
ME stands for the Middle East

explanation.surface: A puzzle over whether a French and Middle Eastern craft is genuinely old.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retained' puts the in-plus-trimmed-doubt run inside QUE plus ME, after its second letter; 'briefly' drops the last letter of QUERY.
explanation.definitionFit: A galley of the ancient Mediterranean with oarsmen in fives, so an old vessel.

clue.text: Point at top, saying "What muscles!"

parts.note: in the exclamation what muscles, what stands for a, as in what a lot of muscle

indicators.note: saying tells us the letters come from how the muscle word is spoken

parts.note: pecs, short for pectorals, are chest muscles

explanation.surface: Someone at the summit admiring a climber's physique.
explanation.walkthrough: 'saying' makes PECS sound as PEX after the A.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest point or tip of something, such as a triangle or mountain, is its peak.

clue.text: Reverse of what regularly taken yoga and diet makes you?

definitions.text: Reverse of what regularly taken yoga and diet makes you?

indicators.note: reverse of says the string of picked letters is read backwards
regularly taken means every other letter is taken from each of the two words

explanation.surface: A wellness question about the effects of yoga and dieting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly taken' picks YG from yoga and DE from diet; 'Reverse of' turns YGDE round. Yoga and diet should make you calm, so the reverse is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The opposite of being calm is being tense and nervous, which this adjective means.

clue.text: Player was skipper of accompanying home team

indicators.note: accompanying puts the departing piece alongside, here after, the home team pieces

parts.note: at home means in
a side is a team
one who skipped out has departed, so was a skipper means went away

explanation.surface: A footballer who used to captain the side that plays at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'skipper' suggests a captain, but here it is one who skips off, i.e. went.
explanation.definitionFit: An old football position between the centre forward and the outside winger, filled by a player.

clue.text: Runner bound to lose footing

indicators.note: to lose footing means the foot of the word, its last letter in a down clue, is dropped

parts.note: to bound is to skip or leap

explanation.surface: A sprinter tied to slip over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runner' suggests an athlete, but a ski is a runner on snow, like a sledge runner.
explanation.definitionFit: A long narrow blade that slides over snow is a runner, as on a sledge.

clue.text: Not so bright —- without the answer?

definitions.text: Not so bright —- without the answer?

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the faded word goes round the other pieces

parts.note: faded colours are less bright than they were

explanation.surface: A remark about someone dim who cannot supply the answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside, not lacking: FADED goes round THE and A. Read whole, the clue is someone dim, short of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Stupid or slow-witted people are not very bright, and a person without the answer is just that.

clue.text: His range of hairpieces, maybe mixed up, require order ultimately

indicators.note: mixed means the letters of the following words are jumbled
ultimately points to the last letter of order

explanation.surface: A tradesman's stock of wigs being muddled, needing to be sorted in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed up' reads as one phrase, but 'mixed' alone is the signal and 'up' joins the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A wigmaker, an old French-derived trade name, is the man whose range of hairpieces it would be.

clue.text: Cheese tart, one unexpectedly holding firm

indicators.note: holding puts the company letters inside the jumbled letters
unexpectedly means the letters turn up in an unexpected order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
Co is short for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A cheese tart that, surprisingly, stays firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unexpectedly' turns TART into RTTA, which holds I and CO after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A soft, mild Italian whey product is a kind of cheese.

clue.text: One nominated to catch others in church summons

indicators.note: in places the playground word inside the church letters

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
in the playground game of tag, whoever is it must catch the other players

explanation.surface: A churchwarden appointed to round up others and hand out summonses.
explanation.definitionFit: To summon someone to appear in a law court is to call them officially, which is one sense of this verb.

clue.text: Stopper one dispatched to vet?

definitions.meaning: something that stops or halts progress, as in chess or a brake
someone sent to inspect and verify, an inspector

explanation.surface: A goalkeeper sent off to the animal doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: one that halts something, and one who inspects or verifies work.

clue.text: Stylish yellow firing range

indicators.note: firing means sacking, so the range word is dismissed from the coward word

parts.note: yellow means cowardly, as does chicken
ken is range of knowledge, as in beyond my ken

explanation.surface: A smart yellow colour scheme at a shooting range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'firing range' looks like a place for shooting, but firing means getting rid of.
explanation.definitionFit: Elegant and fashionable is the meaning of this French-derived adjective.

clue.text: Hard to reverse raising Old Harry

parts.note: H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

indicators.note: raising in a down clue moves the old letter up to the top of the reversing word

parts.note: to undo something is to reverse it

explanation.surface: A struggle to turn back an ageing Harry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old Harry' is a nickname for the Devil, but 'Old' gives O and 'Harry' is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To harry someone is to pester or pursue them relentlessly, as dogs pursue a quarry.

clue.text: Simple door leading to flat

indicators.note: leading to puts the door word in front of the flat word

parts.note: a door is an entry or way in
level means flat

explanation.surface: A plain front door opening into an apartment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flat' looks like an apartment but is the adjective meaning even.
explanation.definitionFit: Basic or suitable for beginners, as with a starter job or product, means simple.

clue.text: That is a bit of a hoot for an audience!

indicators.note: for an audience means the letters follow how the owl call sounds

parts.note: an owl's hoot is traditionally written to-whit to-whoo, so a bit of it is to-whit

explanation.surface: Someone finding something funny and saying so to a crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a bit of a hoot' looks like 'rather funny', but it is part of an owl call.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal phrase meaning namely, used like i.e. or that is to introduce an explanation.

clue.text: Match and small coin placed in dish

indicators.note: placed in puts the coin inside the attractive person

parts.note: a dish is an attractive person, a cutie
p stands for a penny, the small British coin

explanation.surface: A matchstick and a coin dropped into a dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dish' suggests crockery, but it is slang for a good-looking person.
explanation.definitionFit: A knockout game in a football cup competition is a type of match.

clue.text: Variable jokes follow with greeting for those getting everything quickly?

indicators.note: follow puts the variable and jokes after the with and greeting pieces

parts.note: hi is a greeting
in algebra z is a typical variable
to kid is to joke, so kids means jokes

explanation.surface: Assorted gags following a hello, in a talk about fast learners.
explanation.definitionFit: Young prodigies who grasp everything fast are called this, the question mark admitting the definition is loose.

clue.text: All UK constituencies have this troublemaker

parts.note: each UK constituency elects one Member of Parliament, written as I (one) and MP
each UK constituency elects one Member of Parliament, written as I (one) and MP

explanation.surface: A wry remark that every UK seat has its own mischief-maker.
explanation.walkthrough: Every constituency has 1 MP; write 1 as I.
explanation.definitionFit: A mischievous child or little devil is a troublemaker.

clue.text: Close a jacket: one going with collection of books

parts.note: DJ is a dinner jacket
an ace counts as one in cards
NT is the New Testament, a collection of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: An instruction to fasten a jacket, plus a note about a book collection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close' looks like a verb about fastening, but it is the adjective meaning near.
explanation.definitionFit: Close as an adjective means next to or neighbouring, which is the sense of this word.

clue.text: Staff having boarded settle for take-off

indicators.note: having boarded puts the staff inside, like a passenger getting on

parts.note: to settle a bill is to pay it
a rod is a staff or stick

explanation.surface: Airline staff boarding and settling in for take-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take-off' suggests an aircraft leaving, but means a mocking imitation.
explanation.definitionFit: A take-off is an imitation that mocks its original, which is a lampoon or send-up.
